courses.title: Systemic Pharmacology: ANS, CVS and CNS
courses.description: Autonomic drugs, antihypertensives and cardiovascular drugs, drugs for diabetes and endocrine disorders, analgesics, and CNS drugs.

topics.title: Autonomic Pharmacology
topics.summary: Cholinergic and anticholinergic drugs, adrenergic agonists and antagonists.

material.heading: Cholinergic system
material.body: Muscarinic agonists (pilocarpine — glaucoma, dry mouth; bethanechol — urinary retention) mimic parasympathetic effects. Anticholinesterases: reversible (neostigmine — myasthenia gravis, reversal of neuromuscular block; pyridostigmine; physostigmine crosses the BBB; donepezil — Alzheimer's) and irreversible (organophosphates). Organophosphate poisoning causes muscarinic effects (DUMBELS: diarrhoea, urination, miosis, bronchorrhoea/bradycardia, emesis, lacrimation, salivation/sweating), nicotinic effects (fasciculations, weakness) and CNS effects; treat with atropine (titrated to dry secretions) and pralidoxime (early). Antimuscarinics (atropine — bradycardia, premedication; hyoscine butylbromide — abdominal colic; ipratropium and tiotropium — COPD; tropicamide — pupil dilation) cause dry mouth, tachycardia, urinary retention, blurred vision, constipation and confusion ('dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter').

material.heading: Adrenergic system
material.body: Adrenaline (α and β agonist) is first-line for anaphylaxis (IM 0.5 mg of 1:1000 in adults) and cardiac arrest. Noradrenaline (mainly α1, some β1) is a vasopressor in septic shock. Dopamine and dobutamine (β1 — inotrope). Salbutamol (β2 agonist) relieves bronchospasm (side effects: tremor, tachycardia, hypokalaemia). α1 agonist phenylephrine is a decongestant and vasopressor. α-blockers: prazosin and doxazosin (hypertension, BPH), tamsulosin (BPH). β-blockers: propranolol (non-selective — avoid in asthma), atenolol, metoprolol and bisoprolol (β1-selective), carvedilol and labetalol (α + β; labetalol used in pregnancy hypertension); uses include hypertension, angina, heart failure (bisoprolol, carvedilol), arrhythmias, thyrotoxicosis symptoms and migraine prophylaxis; adverse effects include bronchospasm, bradycardia, fatigue, cold extremities and masking hypoglycaemia. Methyldopa (central α2 agonist) is used for hypertension in pregnancy.

topics.title: Antihypertensives and Heart Failure Drugs
topics.summary: Classes of antihypertensives, their adverse effects, and drugs used in heart failure.

material.heading: Antihypertensives
material.body: Main classes: thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, indapamide — hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, hyperuricaemia, hyperglycaemia); calcium channel blockers (dihydropyridines — amlodipine, nifedipine: ankle oedema, flushing, headache; non-dihydropyridines — verapamil, diltiazem: bradycardia, constipation); ACE inhibitors (lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril: dry cough from bradykinin, angioedema, hyperkalaemia, first-dose hypotension; contraindicated in pregnancy and bilateral renal artery stenosis; renoprotective in diabetes); angiotensin receptor blockers (losartan, valsartan — no cough); β-blockers; others (hydralazine, methyldopa, clonidine, spironolactone for resistant hypertension). For Black African patients, a calcium channel blocker or thiazide is usually recommended first-line (often combined), as monotherapy with ACE inhibitors is less effective. Hypertensive emergencies need controlled IV reduction (labetalol, hydralazine, nicardipine).
keyPoints: ACEi: dry cough, angioedema, ↑K; not in pregnancy
Black African patients: CCB or thiazide first

material.heading: Heart failure
material.body: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is treated with drugs that improve survival: ACE inhibitor/ARB or sacubitril–valsartan (ARNI), heart-failure β-blockers (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate — start low, go slow), mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone — monitor potassium) and SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin). Loop diuretics (furosemide) relieve congestion but do not improve survival. Digoxin (inhibits Na+/K+-ATPase, increases vagal tone) controls ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation and reduces hospitalisation; toxicity (nausea, visual disturbance — yellow vision, arrhythmias, bradycardia) is worsened by hypokalaemia and renal impairment. Nitrates (glyceryl trinitrate) relieve angina by venodilation; avoid with sildenafil (severe hypotension).

topics.title: Drugs for Diabetes, Thyroid and Steroids
topics.summary: Insulins and oral hypoglycaemics, thyroid drugs, and corticosteroids.

material.heading: Diabetes drugs
material.body: Insulins: rapid-acting (lispro, aspart), short-acting (soluble/regular — IV in DKA), intermediate (NPH/isophane), long-acting (glargine, detemir) and premixed (70/30); main risks are hypoglycaemia and weight gain. Metformin (biguanide) is first-line for type 2 diabetes: reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis, does not cause hypoglycaemia alone, promotes weight neutrality; side effects are GI upset, vitamin B12 deficiency and rarely lactic acidosis (avoid if eGFR < 30). Sulphonylureas (glibenclamide, gliclazide, glimepiride) stimulate insulin release — hypoglycaemia (glibenclamide especially in the elderly and renal impairment), weight gain. Other classes: DPP-4 inhibitors (sitagliptin), SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin — glycosuria, genital infections, cardio-renal benefit), GLP-1 agonists (liraglutide, semaglutide — weight loss), thiazolidinediones (pioglitazone — fluid retention), acarbose.
keyPoints: Metformin: first-line; no hypoglycaemia alone; B12 deficiency

material.heading: Thyroid and corticosteroids
material.body: Hypothyroidism is treated with levothyroxine (dose titrated to TSH; taken on an empty stomach). Hyperthyroidism: carbimazole (or methimazole) and propylthiouracil (preferred in the first trimester of pregnancy and thyroid storm) inhibit thyroid peroxidase — the serious adverse effect is agranulocytosis (report sore throat or fever immediately); propranolol for symptoms; radioiodine; surgery. Corticosteroids (prednisolone, hydrocortisone, dexamethasone) are anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive; long-term use causes Cushingoid features, hyperglycaemia, hypertension, osteoporosis, infections, peptic ulcer, cataracts, mood changes and adrenal suppression — so they must not be stopped abruptly after prolonged use (risk of Addisonian crisis); give the lowest effective dose and 'sick day' guidance. Dexamethasone is used in preterm labour to mature fetal lungs and in cerebral oedema.

topics.title: Analgesics and Anti-inflammatory Drugs
topics.summary: Paracetamol, NSAIDs, opioids, the WHO analgesic ladder, and gout drugs.

material.heading: Non-opioid analgesics
material.body: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) is analgesic and antipyretic with little anti-inflammatory effect; the adult maximum is usually 4 g/day. Overdose saturates glucuronidation and sulphation, so more is converted by CYP2E1 to the toxic metabolite NAPQI, depleting glutathione and causing hepatic necrosis (risk higher in alcoholics, malnourished patients and enzyme inducers); the antidote is N-acetylcysteine (best within 8 hours, guided by the treatment nomogram). NSAIDs (ibuprofen, diclofenac, naproxen; aspirin) inhibit COX-1 and COX-2, reducing prostaglandins — analgesic, antipyretic and anti-inflammatory; adverse effects: peptic ulceration and GI bleeding, renal impairment, fluid retention, worsening hypertension and heart failure, bronchospasm in aspirin-sensitive asthma, and cardiovascular risk (especially COX-2 selective drugs such as celecoxib). Low-dose aspirin is antiplatelet. Aspirin is avoided in children (Reye's syndrome).
keyPoints: Overdose → NAPQI → liver necrosis; antidote NAC

material.heading: Opioids and gout
material.body: Opioids (morphine, pethidine, tramadol, codeine, fentanyl) act on μ receptors: analgesia, euphoria, respiratory depression, sedation, constipation, nausea and vomiting, miosis, urinary retention, tolerance and dependence. Overdose: pinpoint pupils, coma and respiratory depression — antidote naloxone. Tramadol and codeine misuse is a significant problem among Nigerian youth; NAFDAC restricts high-strength tramadol and codeine syrups. The WHO analgesic ladder: step 1 non-opioid ± adjuvant; step 2 weak opioid (codeine, tramadol); step 3 strong opioid (morphine) — 'by the mouth, by the clock, by the ladder'; always prescribe a laxative with regular opioids. Gout: acute attacks — NSAIDs, colchicine or corticosteroids; long-term urate lowering — allopurinol or febuxostat (xanthine oxidase inhibitors), started after the acute attack settles (initially with prophylaxis); avoid starting allopurinol during an acute attack.
keyPoints: WHO ladder: by mouth, clock, ladder

topics.title: CNS Drugs: Antiepileptics, Antipsychotics, Antidepressants and Anxiolytics
topics.summary: Mechanisms, uses and adverse effects of major psychotropic and antiepileptic drugs.

material.heading: Antiepileptics
material.body: Antiepileptic drugs: carbamazepine (focal seizures, trigeminal neuralgia — enzyme inducer, rash/SJS, hyponatraemia), phenytoin (zero-order kinetics, gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, ataxia, nystagmus, teratogenic), sodium valproate (generalised epilepsy — hepatotoxicity, weight gain, tremor, highly teratogenic — neural tube defects; avoid in women of child-bearing potential unless no alternative), lamotrigine (rash), levetiracetam (mood changes), phenobarbital (widely available, sedative). Status epilepticus (seizure > 5 minutes): IV lorazepam or diazepam (or buccal midazolam/rectal diazepam), then phenytoin/fosphenytoin, levetiracetam or valproate; magnesium sulphate for eclamptic seizures.

material.heading: Psychotropics
material.body: Antipsychotics block dopamine D2 receptors. Typical (haloperidol, chlorpromazine, fluphenazine depot): extrapyramidal side effects (acute dystonia — treat with an anticholinergic such as procyclidine or benzhexol; akathisia; parkinsonism; tardive dyskinesia), hyperprolactinaemia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome (fever, rigidity, autonomic instability, raised CK). Atypical (risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, clozapine — for resistant schizophrenia, risk of agranulocytosis): metabolic syndrome and weight gain. Antidepressants: SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline — first-line; GI upset, sexual dysfunction, hyponatraemia; serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic drugs), tricyclics (amitriptyline — anticholinergic effects, dangerous in overdose from cardiac toxicity). Lithium for bipolar disorder: narrow therapeutic range (≈ 0.4–1.0 mmol/L), toxicity (tremor, ataxia, confusion) worsened by dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and thiazides; causes hypothyroidism and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam) for anxiety, alcohol withdrawal and seizures — dependence and sedation; flumazenil is the antagonist.
keyPoints: Typicals: EPS; treat dystonia with anticholinergic
Lithium: narrow range; toxicity with dehydration
